A robot sleeping at another station does not make this trigger true here. A busy, charging or merely reserved station is not automatically a sleeping station. This trigger has no parameters.

Sleep followed by Wake up robot can prompt another work search after charging has restored the safety reserve, but it cannot create a job, supply tools or bypass a flat battery.
buildcraftrobotics/trigger/linked: Active when this station is taken as a robot's home, whether the robot is docked or away.
Active when this station is taken as a robot's home, whether the robot is docked or away.
<bold>Hint:</bold> A Control Panel link and a robot's home-station link are separate settings.

The home reservation persists while the robot travels to work, supplies or a charger. It does not prove that the robot is currently within sight or ready to work. Temporary visitors do not make a station a home. This trigger has no parameters.

Use Robot in station for physical docking and Station Reserved for any reservation. These meanings concern Docking Stations; they do not describe a Robot Control Panel link.
buildcraftrobotics/trigger/reserved: Active while a robot has taken this station, including a permanent home reservation.
Active while a robot has taken this station, including a permanent home reservation.
<bold>Hint:</bold> Station Reserved does not mean that cargo has been delivered or a charging cycle has finished.

This tests whether the station is claimed. Both a home-linked station and a temporary reservation for travel, loading or charging satisfy it. The robot need not have arrived yet. It does not report arbitrary work-block or item reservations elsewhere.

Use Robot in station when arrival matters. Use Station Linked to distinguish a home link. For predictable local signals, place only one Docking Station on the pipe holding this Gate.
buildcraftrobotics/action/work_filter: Tell your Robot which items or fluids belong in this job.
Sets the home resource filter used by careers that support it.
<bold>Hint:</bold> Keep the filter row active with Always On. When the row becomes inactive its restriction disappears.

Put the Gate on the pipe holding the robot's <bold>home</bold> station. Select Always On followed by Filter and copy a sample into the action parameter. Several nonempty samples in one action form allowed alternatives. Repeated Filter rows in one Gate do not add together: the last active row wins. Without usable samples, the filter is unrestricted.

For a Picker, Carrier or Delivery Robot, use item samples or a List to select handled item types. For a Tank or Pump Robot, use a filled fluid container; empty containers do not identify a fluid. The item or fluid is only a phantom sample and is not consumed.

Block-search workers such as Miner, Lumberjack, Shovelman and Leaf Cutter use <bold>literal block-item samples</bold> to restrict target block types. A List is not expanded into block types there, and an ore's dropped raw item is not the ore block. This filter does not replace a career's own target rules, its work area or its tool filter.
buildcraftrobotics/action/work_filter_to: The correct tool matters just as much as the correct task.
Restricts the held items that the robot may fetch, in addition to its career's requirements.
<bold>Hint:</bold> A tool sample is a filter, not an equipped tool. Put the real usable tool in a provider inventory.

On the home Gate, use Always On followed by Robot tool filter and copy the desired tool or a List into its one parameter slot. The robot still requires a tool valid for its profession, and the provider's Station: provide items rule must also allow the actual stack.

Tool fetching compares item data as well as type where applicable. A sample with different durability or enchantments can prevent a match; use a correctly configured List when broader item matching is intended.

This path also supplies held consumables: Planter seeds, Beekeeper bottles and Stripes items. An old axe-only filter can therefore block those careers. With no usable tool-filter samples, it adds no extra restriction; it does not allow a career to use an unsuitable tool.
buildcraftrobotics/action/goto_station: Sometimes the best instruction is simply to come home.
Orders a robot associated with this station to return here, or move its home to the Docking Station stored in a Map Location parameter.
<bold>Hint:</bold> Use a switchable condition for parking. Always On followed by Robot go to station can keep the robot at home permanently.

Put this action on the home pipe's Gate. With no valid station target parameter, it orders return to this station. To select another dock, record that <bold>station face</bold> in a Map Location and copy the map into the parameter. An area-only map is not a station destination.

The action makes the destination the robot's home and releases the previous home link. Prepare filters and areas on the new home pipe before transferring the robot. It is not a temporary visit or a cargo route.

For a stop switch, use Redstone Signal On followed by Robot go to station with no target. While that signal keeps the action active at the home, the robot returns and stays docked. Switch the signal off to release the hold. Do not simultaneously activate Wake up robot on the same robot, and do not use this as the provider-to-receiver travel instruction: the career handles those trips.
buildcraftrobotics/action/wakeup: An idle Robot might just need a wake-up call.
Lets a sleeping robot leave its sleep state and search for work again.
<bold>Hint:</bold> First fix the missing supply, work area, output route or charge. Waking a robot does not fix those conditions.

Place this action on a Gate at the robot's home or current sleeping dock. It has no parameters. A signal from an inventory or colored wire can wake the robot when work becomes available.

A sleeping robot below its safety energy reserve remains parked until charging restores enough energy. A normal idle robot also retries after its sleep interval, and a Control Panel can notice available work earlier.

Wake up robot clears a control override; do not activate it together with a continuous Robot go to station parking rule. Use mutually exclusive on/off conditions when you need both controls.
buildcraftrobotics/action/work_in_area: An exact work area is better than trusting a Robot to guess.
Uses a saved Map Location area to constrain this home-linked robot's work targets.
<bold>Hint:</bold> Keep the work-area row always active. Making it conditional is not an on/off switch for the robot.

On the home Gate, select Always On followed by Work in Area, then copy a Map Location containing an actual zone into its action parameter. A Zone Planner map paints full-height X/Z columns; a recorded three-dimensional area can also constrain height. A blank or point-only map supplies no valid work zone.

Use one clear Work in Area rule; multiple maps are not automatically merged. Repeated area-setting rows in the same Gate override earlier ones. Make one combined map if a job needs several patches. An inactive or invalid area rule removes that area restriction; it does not tell the robot to stop.

The work area selects job targets and, for Delivery Robots, requesting stations. For a distinct Load/Unload in Area, put that action on a second Gate attached to the same home pipe. These two area actions currently override each other within one Gate. A Control Panel's own work footprint can add another limit for managed robots; it does not replace the home Gate rule.
buildcraftrobotics/action/load_unload_ar: Keep deliveries within the part of the network meant to handle them.
Uses a saved area to limit normal searches for item/fluid loading and unloading stations.
<bold>Hint:</bold> Paint the source and destination pipe positions, not just the chests, tanks or place where the robot hovers.

Put an Always On followed by Load/Unload in Area row on the robot's home Gate and copy a zone Map Location into the action parameter. Use this when a field or construction site has a small work zone but the tool provider and warehouse are outside it.

Without an explicit loading area, normal logistics searches reuse Work in Area. Carrier and Tank routes need both endpoints inside their allowed logistics area. Delivery request destinations are found in the work area, while the supply trip uses the loading area. Charging searches are independent of this restriction.

Multiple maps are not joined automatically. To keep a distinct Work in Area and Load/Unload in Area active together, use two Gates on the same home pipe; the two area actions override each other within one Gate. Some specialized supply paths, including Bomber TNT loading and panel-managed Builder supplies, use their own source selection. Keep station provider and robot-access rules correct as well.
buildcraftrobotics/action/accept_fluids: Tell delivery Robots where they may unload their fluid.
Allows compatible robots to unload selected fluids into this station's Fluid Pipe.
<bold>Hint:</bold> Keep the receiving pipe and tank compatible with the carried fluid, and give the tank enough free space.

Place a station on a Fluid Pipe leading to the receiving tank and attach a Gate to that same pipe. Set Always On followed by Station: accept fluids, with a filled container of the permitted fluid in the parameter.

A Tank Robot requires this accept action. A Pump Robot can also use a plain compatible fluid-pipe station, but explicit accept rules narrow what it may unload there. Several valid samples are alternatives; no recognizable fluid samples means no extra fluid-type restriction.

The action neither empties the tank nor mixes incompatible fluids. The robot can deliver only as much as the destination can accept, and its allowed station area and docking permissions still apply.
buildcraftrobotics/action/accept_items: Tell delivery Robots where their cargo belongs.
Allows compatible robots to unload matching items into this station's Item Pipe.
<bold>Hint:</bold> Use a pipe route with a real storage destination. An accept rule does not reserve space in the final chest.

Place the station on an Item Pipe leading into the receiving inventory. Put Always On followed by Station: accept items on a Gate on the same pipe, and copy an exact allowed item sample into the parameter. Several samples are alternatives; an active action with no nonempty samples accepts any otherwise compatible item. A List is not expanded as a station item sample.

Carriers require an active accept action when choosing a destination. Pickers and some other workers can use a plain non-Wooden Transport Pipe station, but once explicit accept actions are present, their filters govern unloading. A Wooden Transport Pipe needs an explicit accept action to be used as an item-unloading target.

Cargo normally enters the pipe and follows its routing. Keep the pipe connected to storage, with room to accept items; a Gate signal does not guarantee that the downstream system can store the cargo.
buildcraftrobotics/action/forbid_robot: Not every Docking Station should accept every Robot.
Prevents robots matching the configured robot parameters from selecting this station while the action is active.
<bold>Hint:</bold> Check charger access before adding restrictions, so the robot can still reach a compatible charging station.

On the station's Gate, enable Station: forbid robot with one or more robot-filter samples. A programmed <bold>Robot item</bold> selects robots with that career; it is not a unique-robot selector and a loose Redstone Board is not the same sample. A matching wearable item or appropriately configured List can select marked robots.

Use it to exclude a profession or marked robot group. Empty parameters match no robots, so an empty forbid rule does not forbid everyone.

The rule applies while its condition is active. It does not override an occupied station or manufacture a path. Several conflicting allow-only or forbid rules may leave no usable robots; use one clear rule while testing.
buildcraftrobotics/action/force_robot: Reserve this station for the Robots you actually want here.
Allows only robots matching the configured robot parameters to select this station while the action is active.
<bold>Hint:</bold> Check charger access before adding restrictions, so the robot can still reach a compatible charging station.

On the station's Gate, enable Station: force robot with one or more robot-filter samples. A programmed <bold>Robot item</bold> selects robots with that career; it is not a unique-robot selector and a loose Redstone Board is not the same sample. A matching wearable item or appropriately configured List can select marked robots.

Despite its name, this is an allow-only station filter: it does not summon a robot, assign a home or force a work trip. Empty parameters admit no matching robot and can make the station unusable.

The rule applies while its condition is active. It does not override an occupied station or manufacture a path. Several conflicting allow-only or forbid rules may leave no usable robots; use one clear rule while testing.
buildcraftrobotics/action/provide_fluids: Let fluid-carrying Robots know what this station can supply.
Allows compatible robots to drain an advertised fluid from a tank through a Wooden Fluid Pipe station.
<bold>Hint:</bold> Use a filled container such as a Water Bucket as the sample. It selects the fluid without consuming the container.

Aim a Wooden Fluid Pipe at the source tank with a Wrench, add a station on another face and attach a Gate to the same pipe. Enable Always On followed by Station: provide fluids. Put a filled container of the intended fluid in the action parameter.

Up to three fluid samples are supported with sufficient Gate parameter slots. If none of the parameters contains a recognizable fluid, the action adds no fluid-type restriction, so an empty bucket is not a useful filter.

The tank must expose a drainable fluid on the pipe's selected face. The robot's home fluid filter, tank compatibility, allowed loading area and free docking access also apply. Supply actual fluid to the tank; the Gate sample creates none.
buildcraftrobotics/action/provide_items: Mark this station as a source of items for Robot jobs.
Allows robots to take matching real items from the inventory selected by this station's Wooden Transport Pipe.
<bold>Hint:</bold> Aim the Wooden Pipe at the source inventory. The station and its Gate belong on other faces of that same pipe.

Use a Wooden Transport Pipe against the source chest or machine, select its extraction face with a Wrench and add a Docking Station. On a parameter-capable Gate on that pipe, set Always On followed by Station: provide items. Copy an exact item sample into the parameter, such as an Oak Log or the actual tool stack to be supplied.

Up to three samples are supported when the Gate has enough action-parameter slots. Multiple samples are alternatives; with no nonempty samples the active action permits any otherwise eligible item. The robot's home filter and tool requirements still apply. Station samples are exact item comparisons, not expanded Lists.

A phantom sample does not place items in the chest. The inventory must contain extractable stock on the selected face, the robot must be allowed to access it and the station must be free. No engine pulse is needed for the robot's own loading operation.
buildcraftrobotics/action/request_items: Have the Robot network bring materials where they are needed.
Creates item-batch requests for Delivery Robots while the Gate row is active.
<bold>Hint:</bold> Use a Requester block when you want to maintain a target stock count automatically.

On a station mounted to an Item Pipe, enable Station: request items and copy the exact wanted item and count into the action parameter. Each nonempty parameter creates a request. An empty parameter creates no request, and Lists are not expanded into arbitrary requested contents here.

A Delivery Robot finds the request, loads matching stock from a real provider and offers it back at the requesting station. The request amount is a batch size, not a counted target in the downstream inventory. As long as the Gate remains active, the request can be advertised again after delivery.

For bounded replenishment, use an inventory trigger to turn the request off when appropriate, or configure a Requester's phantom target slots. Provide a working output pipe and keep the requesting station in the Delivery Robot's work area.
buildcraftrobotics/action/provide_machin: A machine that needs items can ask Delivery Robots for them.
Identifies machine-request logic in the Gate menu; actual requests must come from a request-capable neighboring block.
<bold>Hint:</bold> A standard Requester already publishes its missing items through an adjacent station.

In the current implementation, a station discovers requests from compatible adjacent blocks directly. Station: machine request is retained as a Gate statement, but switching it on is not required to expose a standard Requester and switching it off does not hide those requests.

It does not make an ordinary chest calculate missing ingredients, craft items or replenish itself. Use a Requester to maintain target stock, or Station: request items for an explicitly gated batch request. The Delivery Robot still needs real provider stock and a valid route.

When several adjacent request-capable blocks are present, station discovery selects one request provider rather than merging every machine into one combined request list. Use separate stations when independent request sources must remain distinct.
buildcraftfactory/item/water_gel: Draining an ocean is effective, but sometimes turning the surface into something solid is the more entertaining solution.
The Water Gelifier converts connected source water and aquatic plants into temporary Water Gel.
<bold>Hint:</bold> Test on a small pool and let the gel finish before harvesting. Breaking it early does not provide Gelled Water.

Use the item while pointing at water. The first gel block is placed at the targeted water position and begins spreading through neighboring source water and supported aquatic plants. Water Gel advances through random ticks, so the randomTickSpeed gamerule directly affects how quickly it spreads and matures. While a non-spreading gel stage is still touching neighboring water it does not advance toward final solidification; once that surrounding water is gone, later random ticks can finish the process.

Only fully solidified Water Gel drops Gelled Water when broken. Earlier spreading or gelling stages do not provide the harvest item. The process is intended for controlled water removal and temporary construction, so test it on a small pool before applying it to an ocean.
buildcraftfactory/item/gel: It looks like water, feels rather less like water and no longer behaves like water at all.
Gelled Water is the solid material recovered from Water Gel.
<bold>Hint:</bold> Harvest the fully solidified stage. Spreading or unfinished Water Gel does not drop Gelled Water.

Use a Water Gelifier on source Water and wait for the connected gel to finish spreading and solidifying. Break the completed gel to obtain Gelled Water. Use the Recipes and Usages sections to check its current crafting roles in your modpack.
buildcraftsilicon/block/laser: Some recipes require precision that a furnace, crafting grid and optimistic hammer cannot provide.
A Laser converts MJ into laser power for nearby compatible BuildCraft tables.
<bold>Hint:</bold> A powered Laser still needs a visible table in front of it with a valid, selected job. A table behind the Laser or hidden by a block will not receive its beam.

Place the Laser within its six-block targeting range and orient its emitting face toward a compatible table. Its search is directional and requires visibility, not an unrestricted sphere around the block. Supply MJ to the Laser and give the table ingredients and a valid selection.

Assembly, Integration and Programming Tables use laser power. Advanced Crafting and Charging Tables also accept MJ directly. A Laser can transfer up to 6.4 MJ/t; several Lasers can work on one table.

A Laser automatically chooses a visible target that can accept energy. If several tables need power, it can switch between them. A missing beam may mean no valid recipe, a blocked output or a fully charged target rather than a broken Laser.
buildcraftsilicon/block/assembly_table: Redstone and diamonds are useful ingredients, but some components require a much more precise arrangement of energy.
The Assembly Table uses laser power to manufacture BuildCraft components and pluggables.
<bold>Hint:</bold> Put an item pipe or inventory beside the table before leaving it to run. Completed items that cannot be accepted are dropped into the world.

1. Insert the ingredients shown by the active recipe display. Click the desired result in the recipe selection area to enable it. Ingredients alone do not select a job.

2. Supply MJ to one or more Lasers facing the table within range. Check that the selected recipe has a nonzero energy target and that its progress increases.

3. Keep an output route beside the table. Finished items are offered to neighboring item pipes first, then inventories; any remainder drops into the world. They are not held in a dedicated internal output buffer.

When several recipes are enabled, the table cycles through eligible jobs. Shared ingredients may be used by any enabled recipe. Recipe choices and costs can be changed by datapacks or addons. Partial energy is stored, but the table clears unused power when it has no valid energy target.
buildcraftsilicon/block/charging_table: A portable machine without energy is merely a decorative machine that is inconvenient to carry.
The Charging Table spends MJ to charge supported energy-storing items.
<bold>Hint:</bold> Robot charging uses a Docking Station on an MJ pipe. This table is for supported energy items; it does not replace a robot charging station.

Place a supported chargeable item in the single slot. Supply MJ directly or with nearby Lasers; the table transfers whole energy units into the item and stops when it cannot accept more. Items without a supported receiving energy store are rejected.

The current table spends <bold>1 MJ per item energy unit</bold>. It does not use the FE Engine / MJ Dynamo conversion ratio. Check the item energy readout and keep this separate from the general default of 10 FE per MJ.

If automation removes the item before it is full, adjust the external extraction rule. The charging slot is accessible for both input and output.
buildcraftsilicon/block/integration_tabl: Some machines are built in one piece. Others become useful only after the important piece is installed.
The Integration Table installs compatible upgrades or components into a target item using laser power.

<bold>Hint:</bold> Compare the result preview with the target before starting. For Gates, material, AND/OR logic and modifier determine different capabilities; copying a program does not upgrade the destination Gate.

Place the target item in the center slot and the required components in the surrounding ingredient slots. A valid integration recipe displays its result. Provide nearby Lasers with MJ and leave room in the output slot; the finished item appears when the recipe has enough energy.

A standard Robotics use is installing a programmed Redstone Board into an empty Robot. That operation requires 5,000 MJ with the bundled recipe. The result is a robot with that career, which still needs a home station, charge and job settings.

An empty preview means the actual target and ingredients do not match an active recipe. A visible preview with no progress calls for checking laser power and output space. Addons and datapacks can change the available integrations.
buildcraftsilicon/block/advanced_craftin: Repeating the same crafting recipe is not difficult, but it is exactly the sort of work a machine should be doing instead.
The Advanced Crafting Table automatically repeats a configured crafting recipe using supplied materials and MJ.
<bold>Hint:</bold> The phantom grid describes the recipe; it does not hold the ingredients being consumed. Put actual materials in the input inventory and keep the output inventory clear.

Arrange the recipe in the phantom 3 by 3 grid, then supply actual matching ingredients to the material inventory. The Recipe Book can fill the phantom grid directly without consuming ingredients.

If several recipes match that grid, left-click the result preview for the next recipe or right-click for the previous one; the choice is saved. Verify the displayed result before automating ingredients.

Supply MJ directly or use nearby powered Lasers. The bundled default cost is 500 MJ per craft. The table needs a valid recipe, sufficient materials, power and output space. Container items and other recipe remainders also need somewhere to go. Use the current recipe preview when a datapack changes a recipe.
buildcraftsilicon/block/programming_tabl: A blank board contains many possibilities and absolutely no useful instructions.
The Programming Table writes a selected robot career onto a blank Redstone Board using laser power.
<bold>Hint:</bold> A programmed board is a career, not a complete robot setup. Install it into a Robot with an Integration Table, then configure the robot home and logistics stations.

Insert a blank Redstone Board, select the desired career and power nearby Lasers facing the table. Leave room in the output slot. The chosen board is produced once the displayed energy cost is reached.

The bundled defaults are 800 MJ for basic logistics; 3,200 MJ for common workers; 12,800 MJ for advanced careers; and 51,200 MJ for Builder. The menu is based on active programming recipes, so datapacks can change costs or offer more than one recipe for a career. Check the selected option rather than assuming every server uses these defaults.

Next, install the board into an empty Robot in an Integration Table. Programming a board does not supply a tool, define an area or provide a charging station.
buildcraftsilicon/item/redstone_crystal: Ordinary redstone dust is energetic, but a crystal is much easier to fit into precision machinery.
A Redstone Crystal is an Assembly Table component used by advanced BuildCraft recipes.
<bold>Hint:</bold> Check both recipes and usages before mass-producing this component. Silicon parts are often shared by several machines, gates and robot upgrades.
Produce Redstone Crystals in an Assembly Table with the ingredients shown by the recipe display. They are used in laser machinery, gates and other high-tier components.
buildcraftsilicon/item/gate_copier: A complicated Gate program is much easier to duplicate than to remember perfectly sixteen times.
The Gate Copier stores one Gate configuration and applies it to compatible Gates.
<bold>Hint:</bold> Keep one verified gate as the master and copy from it. This avoids propagating experimental settings through an entire pipe network.

Right-click a configured Gate with an empty Copier to store its triggers, actions, parameters and row connections. Right-click another Gate with the filled Copier to paste that program. Sneak-right-click in the air to clear the Copier before taking another copy.

Use a destination with sufficient rows and parameter support. The Copier does not change its material, modifier or AND/OR logic; use the same variant when duplicating a tested setup. An incompatible destination is rejected.

Copied directions and parameter values remain the same. Check the station faces, neighboring machines and recorded Maps at the new location. Copying a work-area map also copies the old work area.
buildcraftsilicon/item/plug_timer: A compact pipe network has little room for a tower of repeaters and clocks.
The Timer is a pipe pluggable that adds periodic 5, 10 and 15 second Gate triggers.
<bold>Hint:</bold> Pair a Timer trigger with Single Power Pulse for periodic extraction. A one-tick Timer pulse is not a sustained robot work filter or station permission.

Attach the Timer to a pipe and a Gate to another free face of that pipe. Choose a 5, 10 or 15 second trigger. Each trigger is true for one game tick at its interval; the intervals use world game time, so a newly placed Timer may pulse sooner than a full interval after placement.

The fixed intervals correspond to 100, 200 and 300 ticks. Under server lag, real elapsed seconds can be longer. The Timer blocks its own pipe face and has no separate interval editor.
buildcraftsilicon/item/chipset_red: Every good Gate starts with something more reliable than a pile of redstone dust.
The Red Chipset is the basic redstone logic component used by Gates and other Silicon recipes.
<bold>Hint:</bold> Check both recipes and usages before mass-producing this component. Silicon parts are often shared by several machines, gates and robot upgrades.
Manufacture this chipset in an Assembly Table with laser power. Its exact uses are listed in the recipe display and may include Gates, expansions, Robotics components and laser machinery.
buildcraftsilicon/item/chipset_iron: A stronger Gate calls for a sturdier logic component.
The Iron Chipset is an iron-tier logic component used by stronger Gates and machinery.
<bold>Hint:</bold> Check both recipes and usages before mass-producing this component. Silicon parts are often shared by several machines, gates and robot upgrades.
Manufacture this chipset in an Assembly Table with laser power. Its exact uses are listed in the recipe display and may include Gates, expansions, Robotics components and laser machinery.
buildcraftsilicon/item/chipset_gold: Complex automation needs more than the most basic redstone circuitry.
The Gold Chipset is a gold-tier logic component used by high-capacity Gate and machine recipes.
<bold>Hint:</bold> Check both recipes and usages before mass-producing this component. Silicon parts are often shared by several machines, gates and robot upgrades.
Manufacture this chipset in an Assembly Table with laser power. Its exact uses are listed in the recipe display and may include Gates, expansions, Robotics components and laser machinery.
buildcraftsilicon/item/chipset_quartz: Fine control is easier with a circuit built for precise conditions.
The Quartz Chipset is a quartz logic component used by parameter and timing-oriented recipes.
<bold>Hint:</bold> Check both recipes and usages before mass-producing this component. Silicon parts are often shared by several machines, gates and robot upgrades.
Manufacture this chipset in an Assembly Table with laser power. Its exact uses are listed in the recipe display and may include Gates, expansions, Robotics components and laser machinery.
buildcraftsilicon/item/chipset_diamond: When a Gate needs all its options, a diamond-grade circuit helps.
The Diamond Chipset is the highest standard chipset used by advanced Gate expansions and precision machinery.
<bold>Hint:</bold> Check both recipes and usages before mass-producing this component. Silicon parts are often shared by several machines, gates and robot upgrades.
Manufacture this chipset in an Assembly Table with laser power. Its exact uses are listed in the recipe display and may include Gates, expansions, Robotics components and laser machinery.
buildcraftsilicon/trigger/timer_short: Need a quick signal every five seconds? A Timer can handle that.
This trigger pulses once every 5 seconds while a Timer is attached to the pipe.
<bold>Hint:</bold> This is a brief pulse. Use Single Power Pulse for a periodic extraction request; use a sustained condition for a station permission or robot filter.

The trigger is true for one tick when world game time is divisible by 100. The Timer and Gate must be on the same pipe. All Timers use world time, so placing one does not restart its countdown.

5 seconds assumes 20 game ticks per second; server lag stretches the real interval.
buildcraftsilicon/trigger/timer_medium: For machinery that needs a little more breathing room, try a ten-second interval.
This trigger pulses once every 10 seconds while a Timer is attached to the pipe.
<bold>Hint:</bold> This is a brief pulse. Use Single Power Pulse for a periodic extraction request; use a sustained condition for a station permission or robot filter.

The trigger is true for one tick when world game time is divisible by 200. The Timer and Gate must be on the same pipe. All Timers use world time, so placing one does not restart its countdown.

10 seconds assumes 20 game ticks per second; server lag stretches the real interval.
buildcraftsilicon/trigger/timer_long: Some jobs are worth waiting fifteen seconds between signals.
This trigger pulses once every 15 seconds while a Timer is attached to the pipe.
<bold>Hint:</bold> This is a brief pulse. Use Single Power Pulse for a periodic extraction request; use a sustained condition for a station permission or robot filter.

The trigger is true for one tick when world game time is divisible by 300. The Timer and Gate must be on the same pipe. All Timers use world time, so placing one does not restart its countdown.

15 seconds assumes 20 game ticks per second; server lag stretches the real interval.
buildcrafttransport/pipe/wood_power: A little MJ goes a long way once it leaves the engine.
The Wooden Kinesis Pipe extracts MJ from compatible adjacent energy sources and feeds it into a Kinesis Pipe network.
<bold>Hint:</bold> Use one wooden extraction connection per intended source and avoid closed loops. Verify the source can safely provide the requested MJ rate.

The full default transfer limit is 16 MJ/t. Use this pipe as the intake from an MJ producer; wooden Kinesis intake pipes do not connect directly to one another. Connect an ordinary Kinesis Pipe after the intake to continue the line. Feed a network through a Wooden or Wooden Diamond Kinesis Pipe and put ordinary pipes at consuming machines. Power is distributed among outputs requesting it. The rated limit is a transport ceiling, not energy generation: actual delivery also depends on source output, consumer demand and pipe resistance. Crude Oil is the starting fluid for BuildCraft refining and a usable dirty fuel. Its temperature selects both its distillation route and its engine output. <bold>Hint:</bold> Keep the incoming oil, both Distiller outputs and engine residue in separate lines. A backed-up by-product can stop an otherwise powered refinery.
Oil deposits generate in the world and can be collected with Buckets, a Pump or other compatible fluid handlers. Store it in Tanks and move it with Fluid Pipes.

<bold>Built-in fuel values:</bold> One bucket is 1,000 mB.
Cool: 3 MJ/t; 30,000 MJ per bucket.
Hot: 3.75 MJ/t; 37,500 MJ per bucket.
Searing: 4.5 MJ/t; 45,000 MJ per bucket.

Burn duration is unchanged by temperature. Hot and Searing variants produce 1.5 and 2 times the Cool variant's engine heat per tick. Each bucket produces 125 mB of Cool Residue at every fuel temperature; drain it to keep the engine running.

These are the default fuel profiles. Server datapacks or addons may change them; processing energy is not deducted from the totals.

<bold>Refining:</bold> Cool Oil separates into Gaseous Fuel and Heavy Oil. Hot Oil separates into Mixed Light Fuel and Dense Oil. Searing Oil separates into Distilled Oil and Residue. Both outputs retain the input temperature. Use a Heat Exchanger when the next recipe needs a different temperature.

Residue has Cool, Hot and Searing forms. A Heat Exchanger can move it between adjacent temperature states, so hot residue can take part in heat exchange before storage or disposal. buildcraftcompat/pipe/propolis_item: Sorting bees by color was never going to be precise enough for a serious apiary.
The Apiarist's Pipe is a Forestry compatibility item pipe that routes genetic items with a separate filter for every side.
<bold>Hint:</bold> Use an Apiarist's Pipe at a dedicated bee-processing junction. Keep a normal overflow route so unexpected bee types do not block the network.

Open the pipe and configure each output face with Forestry's genetic filter rules, including species and life-stage choices. The species selections refine the rule for that face; the interface can store up to three selections per side.

Specifically matching rules take priority over an Anything route. If several outputs satisfy the same priority, normal pipe routing chooses among them; this is not a fixed first-side-wins sorter. Use an Anything output for deliberate overflow rather than assuming an unconfigured face accepts every bee.

Test the relevant drones, princesses, queens or other genetic items before enabling bulk transfer. A filter does not reserve inventory room at the destination. This page is available only where Forestry and the matching compatibility pipe are installed.
buildcraftenergy/block/engine_fe: An existing FE network is a perfectly good place to get the power for a BuildCraft factory.
The FE Engine consumes Forge Energy, converts it into MJ and behaves as a directional BuildCraft engine.
<bold>Hint:</bold> Use the FE Engine when an FE network should power an MJ-only BuildCraft network without enabling automatic conversion for every ordinary machine.

FE enters on the faces other than the moving MJ output. The input buffer holds 10,000 FE; the MJ buffer holds 1,000 MJ. Base production is 4 MJ/t, which consumes up to 40 FE/t at the default ratio of 1 MJ = 10 FE. The dedicated converter works in MJ_ONLY as well as the automatic-conversion modes. On Fabric, compatible external energy is exposed through TeamReborn Energy. The FE labels in this guide refer to that external-energy side as well.

The four upgrade slots each accept one Iron or Gold Gear. Each Iron Gear adds 2 MJ/t; each Gold Gear adds 3 MJ/t. Four Iron Gears give 12 MJ/t; four Gold Gears give 16 MJ/t. At the default ratio those rates consume up to 120 or 160 FE/t. Upgrades increase conversion speed, not energy gained from each FE. The configured power.mjPerFe ratio determines the cost; a lack of input energy or output space reduces actual conversion.

Connect an FE source or FE delivery pipe to a non-output face, point the moving end at an MJ consumer or Wooden Kinesis Pipe, then apply redstone. If an MJ line does not connect, check that its input is a Wooden or Wooden Diamond Kinesis Pipe.

The engine converts only as much FE as fits in the MJ buffer. A partially filled buffer can accept a smaller conversion; a full buffer makes it wait. Keep an outlet available and monitor the engine's heat during sustained operation.
buildcraftenergy/block/mj_dynamo: Sometimes a machine needs FE, but the rest of the workshop runs on MJ.
The MJ Dynamo consumes BuildCraft MJ and produces Forge Energy through its directional output face.
<bold>Hint:</bold> Feed MJ into a non-output face and point the moving end at an FE consumer or a Wooden FE Pipe. Ordinary FE transport pipes are not source intake pipes.

The Dynamo holds 1,000 MJ and 10,000 FE. MJ enters on non-output faces; FE leaves through the facing/output side. Base conversion is up to 4 MJ/t, giving 40 FE/t at the default 1 MJ = 10 FE ratio. The dedicated converter remains available in MJ_ONLY. On Fabric, compatible external-energy connections use TeamReborn Energy. The direction and upgrade rules are the same.

Each of the four upgrade slots accepts one Iron or Gold Gear. Iron adds 2 MJ/t of conversion capacity; Gold adds 3 MJ/t. Four Iron Gears give up to 12 MJ/t converted, and four Gold Gears give 16 MJ/t: 120 or 160 FE/t at the default ratio. Upgrades change conversion speed; the configured MJ/FE ratio determines the energy exchanged.

Apply redstone to enable conversion and use a Wrench to choose the FE output face. The Dynamo converts only the amount of MJ whose FE result fits in the buffer; it can perform a smaller final conversion rather than overflowing it.

For a pipe-fed FE network, place a Wooden or Wooden Diamond FE Pipe at the output, followed by ordinary FE transport pipes and a consumer. When redstone is off, stored FE slowly self-discharges by 1 FE per tick, so the Dynamo is not a long-term battery. If output stops, check facing, the receiving pipe type, consumer demand and available MJ.
buildcrafttransport/pipe/wood_fe: An FE source is only useful when its energy reaches a network that can carry it.
The Wooden FE Pipe extracts FE from an adjacent energy source and injects it into the FE-pipe network.
<bold>Hint:</bold> Put extraction pipes only on actual FE providers and size the next segment for the same load. A fast source cannot push through a slower downstream bottleneck.

Default transfer limit: 160 FE/t. FE rates scale with pipes.baseFeRate, whose default is 40 FE/t. The setting does not change MJ-pipe rates or the MJ/FE conversion ratio. Place this intake against an FE source, then connect ordinary FE transport pipes and a consumer. It can take FE from a source that allows extraction or receive FE offered into its source connection. Wooden FE intake pipes do not connect directly to each other. No MJ pulse or engine is required to make them extract FE. The network transfers according to consumer demand, available energy and the slowest segment. It transports external energy and performs no MJ conversion by itself. FE Pipes remain available in MJ_ONLY; use an FE Engine or MJ Dynamo where the energy type must change. Fabric connections use compatible TeamReborn Energy storage.

The Cobblestone FE Pipe is the basic low-capacity FE transport pipe.
<bold>Hint:</bold> FE throughput is limited by the slowest segment in the route. Upgrade the busy trunk before spending high-tier pipes on lightly loaded branches.

Default transfer limit: 40 FE/t. FE rates scale with pipes.baseFeRate, whose default is 40 FE/t. The setting does not change MJ-pipe rates or the MJ/FE conversion ratio. Use a Wooden or Wooden Diamond FE Pipe at the energy source and this pipe to carry power toward compatible consumers. Ordinary transport pipes are not a substitute for the wooden source intake. Stone and Cobblestone FE Pipes do not connect directly to each other. The network transfers according to consumer demand, available energy and the slowest segment. It transports external energy and performs no MJ conversion by itself. FE Pipes remain available in MJ_ONLY; use an FE Engine or MJ Dynamo where the energy type must change. Fabric connections use compatible TeamReborn Energy storage.

The Stone FE Pipe is a general low-capacity FE transport pipe.
<bold>Hint:</bold> FE throughput is limited by the slowest segment in the route. Upgrade the busy trunk before spending high-tier pipes on lightly loaded branches.

Default transfer limit: 80 FE/t. FE rates scale with pipes.baseFeRate, whose default is 40 FE/t. The setting does not change MJ-pipe rates or the MJ/FE conversion ratio. Use a Wooden or Wooden Diamond FE Pipe at the energy source and this pipe to carry power toward compatible consumers. Ordinary transport pipes are not a substitute for the wooden source intake. Supply usable shears through Station: provide items. Set Work in Area around the flock and Load/Unload in Area around the provider if it lies outside the field. Robot tool filter can select the shears to fetch.

The robot shears adult sheep that have regrown their wool, using the normal interaction and consuming tool durability. It does not shear babies or already-sheared sheep, and it does not breed, feed or attack them. Wool drops naturally for a Picker to collect.

buildcraftcore/item/redstone_control_mod: An emergency lever is useful only when the machine is actually listening to it.
The Redstone Controlling Module adds a redstone enable requirement to five supported BuildCraft machines.
<bold>Hint:</bold> Removing the module removes the redstone requirement. A machine that still has power and work can resume immediately.

Right-click a Builder, Filler, Quarry, Mining Well or Pump with the module to install it. One module is consumed outside creative mode. It is an upgrade to the machine itself, not a pipe pluggable.

Use a Wrench on a machine with a module to remove and recover it. This interaction takes precedence over ordinary wrench rotation while the module is installed. The module is also included in normal machine drops.

Without a module, these five machines do not need ordinary redstone power to run. With the module installed, they require a neighboring redstone signal. Removing that signal pauses work; it does not create MJ or provide materials. Other machine requirements still apply.

For a Pump mounted on a Quarry, the Quarry enable condition also matters. The Flood Gate has its own redstone behavior and is not one of these five machines.

Install the module in the target machine. Put a pipe with a Gate beside it and use a suitable condition -> Redstone Signal. When the condition is false, the signal stops and the module pauses the machine.

Test with a lever first, then replace the lever with the Gate condition. A supported On/Off machine-mode action is a separate control mechanism; installing this module does not add every machine-mode action to every block.
buildcraftlib/config/bcce_settings: Before rebuilding a working factory to match a number in a book, check which rules the world is using.
BCCE has its own settings editor for client preferences, world rules, machine balance and registered addon options.
<bold>Hint:</bold> Text in this book describes bundled defaults. Use the live recipe, machine display and setting tooltip when a pack changes the balance.

On Forge or NeoForge, use Mods -> BuildCraft -> Config. On Fabric, the optional Mod Menu integration opens the same BCCE editor.

Inside a world, assign Open BuildCraft settings under Options -> Controls -> Key Binds -> BuildCraft. It has no default key. The binding works when another screen is not open.

Client changes local presentation, such as display units, pipe item rendering and book page memory. World/Server changes gameplay rules. Balance contains machine, robot and energy values. The Addons/BCCE view switch selects whose settings are shown; it does not change which world they belong to.

In singleplayer, World and Balance use the installation personal profile shared by personal worlds. On a dedicated server, those settings belong to the connected server and require the appropriate operator permission. Changing client preferences does not change a server recipe or machine limit.

Search for the setting name, expand its category and read the tooltip for the default, limits and application rule. Edits and resets are staged until Done; Cancel discards them.

Some display options apply immediately. Most world rules and balance changes require a world/server restart; follow the rule shown for the setting. Reopening a machine GUI is not a substitute for a required restart.

If a remote settings save is rejected because the server changed in the meantime, reopen the editor and review the current values before applying the change again.

Check the actual recipe selected by the machine, then the relevant Balance entry, power mode and world enable controls. Datapacks and addons may change recipes independently of the settings editor.

Examples: Marker reach belongs to Markers balance; pump range and water-source consumption belong to Pump balance; robot costs and limits belong to Robotics balance. The old loader TOML and machine INI files are migration inputs, not the current settings interface.
buildcrafttransport/trigger/power_reques: A powered factory is only useful when its machines actually need the energy.
Power Requested is a Gate trigger for current demand in the attached MJ Kinesis or FE pipe.
<bold>Hint:</bold> Demand is not proof of delivery. This trigger can be on while the generator is empty or switched off.

Put the Gate on a Kinesis or FE line. Power Requested is true when that pipe reports positive demand; it needs no item or fluid parameter. It checks the attached energy network rather than a nearby fuel inventory.

Use it as one input to generator control or a status signal. Keep the generator's own cooling and fuel behavior in mind: a Stirling fuel item continues burning after redstone is removed, and a Combustion Engine has a cooling lockout after shutdown. Rapid demand changes are therefore a poor reason to repeatedly restart those engines.

Check that a consumer is connected and able to accept energy, the route is not disabled by a limiter, the source uses the correct Wooden intake pipe, and both ends are in loaded chunks. A full machine or a blocked route can have no current demand even though the network was working earlier.
buildcraftrobotics/config/gate_setup: Build one complete route before adding a fleet: a working home, supplies and a destination make each later robot easier to configure.
This walkthrough explains where each robot Gate belongs and gives complete Carrier and tree-farm setups using the current station rules.
<bold>Hint:</bold> Keep one Docking Station per pipe block, leave clear air outside its face and test with one robot before sharing service stations.

<bold>Home:</bold> the station where the Robot was deployed, or the new home selected with Robot go to station. Its Gate supplies Work in Area, Load/Unload in Area, Filter and Robot tool filter. These govern the robot while it is away.

<bold>Provider:</bold> a station on a Wooden Item or Fluid Pipe aimed at the source inventory or tank. Its Gate says what resources robots may take.

<bold>Acceptor:</bold> a station on a transport pipe leading to the destination. Its Gate says what cargo robots may unload.

<bold>Charger:</bold> a station on an MJ Kinesis Pipe carrying engine power. A home may also be the charger. An Item, Fluid, Structure or FE pipe does not become a charger merely because a station is installed on it.

1. Install the Docking Station first. Install the Gate on a different face of that <bold>same pipe block</bold>, then open the Gate. A neighboring pipe's Gate is not this station's Gate.

2. Choose the trigger on the left and the action on the right. To select a statement, press and hold the left mouse button, move to the desired choice and release. Use Always On for permanent filters, areas and provider permissions.

3. If the action needs a parameter, use a Gate with action-parameter slots and click the parameter with the item or saved Map Location on your cursor. The Gate keeps a phantom copy; it does not consume or supply that item.

4. Use separate, unjoined rows for separate rules. AND/OR connectors combine trigger conditions; they are not steps in a program. Do not join every Always On row just to make several actions run.

A Quartz modifier gives one action parameter per row, Diamond up to three. Gold Quartz has four rows, which fits a useful home setup. Put the sample in the action parameter, not the trigger parameter. Repeated settings in one Gate use the last active row. In particular, Work in Area and Load/Unload in Area currently conflict within a single Gate; put them on two Gates attached to the same home pipe when you need both.

This starter system has <bold>two cargo stations and one charging home</bold>. Put them a few blocks apart on loaded terrain. The robot carries items between them; the two cargo pipes need no direct connection.

<bold>Home H:</bold> place a Stirling Engine, give it suitable furnace fuel and enable it with a redstone signal. Aim it into a Wooden Kinesis Pipe, then connect a short Stone Kinesis Pipe segment. These are MJ power pipes. Put the Docking Station on the Stone segment with an unobstructed approach, and a Gold Quartz Gate on another face. Keep the engine fueled and enabled during operation.

<bold>Source A:</bold> put Oak Logs in a chest. Place a Wooden Transport Pipe against it and use a Wrench to aim the extraction face at the chest. Place a station on another pipe face and a parameter-capable Gate on a third. Leave the station approach clear. The robot loads directly from that chest; do not add a Pulsar or engine for this loading step.

<bold>Destination B:</bold> put a Stone Transport Pipe against an empty destination chest, with a station and a parameter-capable Gate on free faces. Make sure the pipe has a route into the chest.

<bold>At A:</bold> Always On followed by Station: provide items, with an Oak Log sample.

<bold>At B:</bold> Always On followed by Station: accept items, with an Oak Log sample.

<bold>At H, row 1:</bold> Always On followed by Filter, with an Oak Log sample. This restricts the robot's cargo.

<bold>At H, row 2:</bold> Always On followed by Load/Unload in Area, with a zone Map Location covering the pipe positions of both A and B. Create it with the Zone Planner, select the painted layer and export it before copying it into the Gate.

A parameter-capable Gate such as Iron Quartz can hold the one rule at each cargo station. Keep the home rows unjoined. For this item route a separate Work in Area row is not needed: the important station restriction is Load/Unload in Area. The charger is found independently of that area.

Program a Carrier board, integrate it into an empty Robot and use that Robot on H. H is now its home and charging dock. Verify that its charge actually rises while docked; the first charge with one Stirling Engine can take time. A station on an empty MJ pipe is still recognized as a charger, so the pipe type alone does not prove that power is arriving. Once it has sufficient energy and the route is valid, it should travel to A, load logs, fly to B and insert them into B's pipe. The destination chest should gain the same real logs that left the source.

If it stays at H, first check that charge is increasing and that the Stirling Engine still has fuel, a redstone signal and the correct facing. Then check the source Wooden Pipe direction, the real logs in the chest and whether both Gate rules are active. If it loads but cannot unload, check B's accept sample, pipe connection and chest capacity. If a station is never selected, check the map includes the <bold>pipe coordinates</bold>, that the station is not another robot's home and that its front is reachable.

For a fluid route, replace the Carrier with a Tank Robot, A with a Wooden Fluid Pipe against the source tank and B with a Fluid Pipe into a receiving tank. Use Station: provide fluids and Station: accept fluids with filled-container samples, and replace the Oak Log in the home Filter with the same filled container, for example a Water Bucket. Keep the charging home and redraw the logistics map if the endpoint pipe positions move.

Give a Lumberjack its own powered home, a Wooden Transport Pipe tool-provider station beside a chest of axes, and an item-pipe output station leading to storage. A separate Picker uses the output; a separate Planter can replace saplings. Each robot needs its own home reservation.

<bold>Lumberjack home row 1:</bold> Always On followed by Work in Area, with a map covering the trees.

<bold>Second Gate on the same Lumberjack home pipe:</bold> Always On followed by Load/Unload in Area, with a map including the axe provider. Use a second Gate because Work in Area and Load/Unload in Area override each other within one Gate.

<bold>Lumberjack first Gate, row 2:</bold> Always On followed by Robot tool filter, with the intended axe or a List configured to match usable replacement axes.

<bold>Tool-provider Gate:</bold> Always On followed by Station: provide items, with the actual supplied axe sample. For a dedicated chest containing only permitted axes, leave the action sample empty to allow the home tool filter and career requirement to choose among them. Different durability or enchantments can affect an exact sample.

The Lumberjack cuts logs and leaves drops. Configure the Picker's home with the tree patch as Work in Area. If its output station is outside that patch, use a second home Gate for Load/Unload in Area; enable Station: accept items at the output. The Picker collects and stores the logs. For replanting, supply saplings and give the Planter its own work and loading areas.

To park a robot, add a home rule with Redstone Signal On followed by Robot go to station and leave its destination empty. Put a lever where it powers the home pipe. When the condition is true, the robot returns to that home and remains docked while the command continues. Turn the lever off to release the hold.

Keep area and filter rows on Always On during this stop/start arrangement. If Work in Area is enabled only by the lever, switching the lever off <bold>removes the boundary</bold> rather than safely stopping work.

Wake up robot can prompt a sleeping robot after useful work appears, but it cannot supply energy or missing tools. Do not make Wake up robot and Robot go to station active at the same time. A Map Location targeting another station in the return action deliberately changes home, so the new home must already have the intended rules.
When a Rule Seems to Do Nothing

<bold>No robotics actions:</bold> the Gate must share a pipe with a station, and its variant must have enough action-parameter slots for the chosen action.

<bold>No tools or cargo:</bold> the provider must be a correctly aimed Wooden transport pipe with an active provide action and real extractable stock. Check exact item data and the home filters.

<bold>Works outside the expected patch:</bold> the map must contain an area, be in the home action parameter and remain active. Point-only maps do not define areas. Zone Planner paint covers all heights.

<bold>Never reaches a provider:</bold> without a separate loading area, normal supply searches inherit Work in Area. Put service stations in their own allowed area when necessary.

<bold>Always returns or sleeps:</bold> check an active return command, battery charge, free charger, eligible work, protected targets and a clear flight path. Sleeping can simply mean that no eligible work exists.

<bold>Another robot takes the station:</bold> use free service stations and suitable Station: force robot or Station: forbid robot parameters. A programmed Robot sample matches a career, not one unique robot.
buildcraftrobotics/block/robot_processor: A larger workforce benefits from a shared work map and a clear view of who is waiting for what.
The Robot Control Panel coordinates explicitly linked robots, tracks their tasks and cargo, and stores its setup on an HDD. The item is marked Experimental.
<bold>Hint:</bold> Make the robot's station-and-Gate setup work first. The panel does not replace its career board, provider rules, tools or charging stations.

Place the panel, insert one Hard Disk Drive and supply MJ directly through a suitable power connection. Its buffer holds 5,000 MJ. With loaded linked robots, its current power budget is 8 MJ/t plus 2 MJ/t per robot, up to 40 MJ/t for sixteen robots. With none loaded it has no scheduling draw, but it still needs charge to become operational for setup.

Sneak-use a Robot Controller on the panel to bind the controller. Then sneak-use that controller on each robot and each desired station face to add them explicitly. Nearby robots are not added automatically. The panel supports up to sixteen robots and sixty-four station links. You must have permission to manage a robot. A robot newly linked to another panel belongs to that new controller rather than two panels at once.

The panel uses a 112 by 112 block work footprint. A fresh disk aligns it to the seven-by-seven chunk square around the panel. Paint colored layers to limit managed work within that footprint; the painted layers form a combined area. If no layer is painted, the whole footprint is allowed. The colors do not assign careers or separate teams.

Home Gate work areas, filters and tool requirements still apply. The panel shares discovery and schedules suitable work; it does not authorize mining outside a robot's Gate area or remove owner permission checks. Keep provider and destination station rules configured, and explicitly link the stations used by managed logistics.

Only loaded world data is scanned. The footprint does not mean that all seven-by-seven chunks are permanently force-loaded. Moving the panel or HDD also requires checking station coordinates and the resulting work map.

Select a robot to see its career, task, charge, status and available cargo. The cargo display is read-only; dragging or scrolling it does not transfer items. Switch to the station list to inspect linked coordinates, faces and occupancy. Names can be changed with Enter to save or Esc to cancel. Unlinking removes the panel association without destroying the robot or station.

Home orders the selected robot back to its home station. Shift plus Home requests a temporary load of its last known chunk, subject to server chunk-loading settings and limits. It is a recovery aid, not permanent loading of the whole work area.

The execution queue limit is one to eight jobs per supported worker, five by default, and includes the current job. A connected tree or ore vein counts as one job. A longer queue does not make an individual robot perform several physical actions simultaneously. Use task and waiting information to distinguish missing materials, charging, unreachable work and a genuinely empty work area.

The HDD stores the panel's painted areas, links, names and queue settings. Removing it or losing MJ stops central scheduling and disables panel editing; it is <bold>not a universal robot stop switch</bold>. Robots can return to their ordinary board behavior using their home Gates. Use a sustained home Gate return command when they must stay parked.

An unreadable disk is not silently reformatted. Keep the disk and inspect its state rather than expecting the panel to rebuild missing setup automatically. The Controller also needs the panel to be loaded in the same dimension before it can open it remotely.
buildcraftrobotics/item/controller: A remote control is useful only after you tell it which panel and workers belong together.
The Robot Controller binds robots and stations to a Robot Control Panel and opens that panel remotely.
<bold>Hint:</bold> Insert the panel's HDD and supply MJ before linking workers. The controller does not power the panel or load its chunk.

1. Sneak-use the Controller on the Robot Control Panel. It stores that panel's position and dimension.

2. Sneak-use the bound Controller on a robot to link that robot, provided you have management permission. Linking it to a different panel moves its controller association.

3. Sneak-use it on the actual face occupied by a Docking Station to add that station. Clicking an arbitrary pipe face without a station does not create a link.

A Control Panel link is separate from the robot's home. This procedure does not reassign its home station, change its board or replace its Gate rules.

Use the bound Controller normally in the air to open the stored panel. The panel must still exist, be loaded and be in your current dimension. There is no automatic scan for replacement panels or nearby robots.

If it reports that the panel is missing or unloaded, load or restore the original panel, or deliberately bind the Controller to the intended new one. Use the panel's own unlink controls to remove robot or station associations.
buildcraftrobotics/item/hard_disk: The panel supplies computing power; the HDD carries the saved setup.
A Hard Disk Drive is the non-stackable storage medium required by the Robot Control Panel.
<bold>Hint:</bold> Keep the original HDD when moving a configured panel. A new blank disk is a different setup.

Insert one HDD into the panel's disk slot. A blank disk is initialized by the panel; a valid used disk loads its saved work layers, map name, linked robots, station positions, names and execution queue limit. Supply MJ to edit and use the panel.

The disk contains configuration, not robots, cargo, fuel or battery charge. Taking it out stops the panel's scheduling and removes that setup from the active panel until a suitable disk is inserted. The robots themselves remain in the world.

The painted 112 by 112 work footprint is stored relative to the panel position, so it moves with the disk's installation location. Robot and station links retain their identities and coordinates; moving the disk does not teleport them. Check every station link and the map before restarting a relocated setup. Links also belong to the recorded dimension.

An explicitly relinked robot belongs to its newer controller; an old disk does not automatically reclaim it. If a disk is reported invalid, its unreadable data is preserved instead of silently formatted. A blank replacement can start a new setup, but it does not recover the old configuration.
